Running total: 2026 vs 2025 Tracker totals differ by methodology. Layoffs.fyi counted roughly 173,900 tech workers laid off in 2026 as of early August; Yahoo Tech's tracker put the figure near 165,000, and narrower counts sit around 153,000. The realistic range as of August 5 is 153,000 to 174,000. For comparison, 2025 closed at roughly 245,000 tech layoffs; 2026 reached the 150,000 mark faster than 2025 did, so the year is on pace to match or exceed it. Q1 2026 alone accounted for about 82,000 cuts. Monthly timeline, January to August 2026 January. Amazon opened the year with roughly 16,000 corporate role eliminations — about 30,000 combined with its October 2025 round — the largest confirmed announcement of early 2026. February. Cuts continued at a steady pace across mid-size software firms as Q1 accumulated toward its ~82,000 total; Oracle's March 31 mass layoff was still ahead at that point. March. Dell confirmed roughly 11,000 job cuts in a late-March reduction that took headcount from about 108,000 to 97,000. April. Just under 12,000 workers were let go across companies including Disney's technology units, Amazon follow-on cuts, and Snap, per Yahoo Tech's monthly tally . May. Meta laid off 8,000 employees effective May 20, about 10% of its workforce, and canceled 6,000 open requisitions, framing the cuts as funding for its AI programs, per Al Jazeera . June. About 14,000 cuts were logged across Lucid, Bungie, Robinhood, and others; individual company figures were not broken out in most cases. July. The busiest month of the summer: Microsoft cut 4,800 roles with Xbox hit hardest (~3,200), Monday.com eliminated ~630 positions (20%) in an AI platform pivot, Samsung cut 839 US roles including its New Jersey headquarters relocation, and Intel's manufacturing layoffs of up to 20% of that workforce began taking effect. August. Magic Leap filed a WARN notice covering 193 jobs at its Florida headquarters, effective October 1, as it exits the headset business. Year-to-date totals crossed the 165,000 mark on broad-count trackers. Why the cuts are happening Companies cite AI restructuring more than any other reason. Meta, Monday.com, and Salesforce all tied their 2026 reductions directly to AI product pivots or AI-funded reorganizations. Analyses of Q1 announcements attribute roughly 42% of cuts to restructuring and 39% to budget reallocation toward AI projects. Intel and Dell cite cost reduction after revenue pressure; Samsung and Magic Leap cite site consolidation and business-model exits. The counterweight is documented in hiring data: while these cuts ran, hiring for AI-related positions rose about 92%, and Indeed Hiring Lab found AI-mentioning postings growing against otherwise weak tech hiring. US AI-related vacancies reached 55,374 in Q1 2026, up 36% year over year. The same companies cutting general engineering, support, and marketing roles are posting AI engineering roles at record rates. Biggest tech layoffs of 2026, ranked Oracle — ~20,000–30,000 reported (March 31; total unconfirmed) Amazon — ~16,000 (January; ~30,000 combined with the October 2025 round) Intel — 2026 total undisclosed (more than 35,000 roles cut since 2024) Microsoft — 4,800 (July 6, Xbox-heavy) Dell — ~11,000 (March) Meta — 8,000 (May, ~10%) Wix — ~1,000 (~20%) LinkedIn — ~875 (5%) Samsung — 839 US roles (July) Monday.com — ~630 (July, 20%) What happens to the IT teams left behind Layoff rounds rarely reduce the systems an IT department is responsible for; they reduce the people responsible for them. Surviving staff absorb the patching, backup, monitoring, and ticket queues of eliminated colleagues, and specialist coverage — database administration, Exchange, virtualization — is often the first depth lost. The documented industry response is outsourcing: companies that cut internal IT contract managed services providers to cover the workload that did not disappear with the headcount. This pattern held in the 2023-2024 cycle and is repeating in 2026, with server and helpdesk support the most commonly externalized functions. Aggregate totals reference layoffs.fyi and outlet trackers and are presented as ranges where trackers disagree. Reported-but-unconfirmed rounds are listed in the exclusions note, not the table. This page is updated monthly; the date stamp at the top reflects the last revision. FAQ How many tech layoffs have there been in 2026? Between roughly 153,000 and 174,000 as of August 5, 2026, depending on tracker methodology. Layoffs.fyi counts about 173,900; narrower trackers count about 153,000. Which company cut the most jobs in 2026? By reported size, Oracle’s March 31 mass layoff (20,000–30,000 reported, unconfirmed by the company). Amazon’s January round (~16,000) is the largest company-confirmed single announcement of 2026. Why are tech companies laying off employees? The most-cited reasons are AI restructuring and budget reallocation toward AI programs, followed by conventional cost reduction and site consolidation. Analyses of 2026 announcements attribute about 42% to restructuring and 39% to AI-directed budget shifts. Will layoffs continue through 2026? Announced plans indicate yes. Meta has flagged additional cuts for the second half of 2026, Intel's manufacturing reductions run through year-end, and Magic Leap's WARN-filed cuts take effect October 1. The year's pace is ahead of 2025, which finished at about 245,000. The moves come as the Bay Area shed 2,000 tech jobs in June, sparking worries that enterprise SaaS budgets may tighten as companies curb spending amid broader market pressure. Why It Matters The layoffs at Intel and Uber highlight a macro‑level shift in tech spending that directly impacts SaaS providers. As headline hiring slows, SaaS firms that depend on expanding user bases within large enterprises may see a dip in net‑new ARR, forcing them to double down on retention and expansion strategies. This dynamic could accelerate a broader industry move toward consumption‑based pricing and tighter ROI validation, reshaping GTM playbooks across the sector. Additionally, the Bay Area’s employment contraction serves as a bellwether for other tech hubs. If similar patterns emerge in other regions, SaaS vendors could face a sustained period of budget restraint, prompting a reevaluation of growth forecasts and capital allocation decisions among investors and operators alike. Key Points Intel cuts 103 jobs in Santa Clara, effective Aug. 15, 2026 Uber eliminates 41 positions in San Francisco, effective Sept. 21, 2026 Combined layoffs total 144 jobs, filed via California WARN notices Bay Area tech sector shed ~2,000 jobs in June 2026, indicating broader contraction SaaS vendors may face tighter enterprise budgets, prompting a shift toward retention and consumption‑based pricing Analysis The Intel‑Uber layoffs are less about the individual companies and more about the health of the enterprise software market that underpins them. Historically, SaaS growth has been tightly coupled with tech hiring cycles; a surge in headcount drives demand for collaboration, security, and analytics tools, while a contraction can quickly reverse that trend. The current cuts, though modest in absolute numbers, arrive at a time when the Bay Area—a traditional engine of SaaS adoption—is already feeling the strain of a 2,000‑job monthly bleed. This suggests that SaaS vendors should anticipate a deceleration in net‑new ARR and prepare for heightened scrutiny of spend at the CFO level. From a strategic standpoint, operators will likely accelerate product‑led growth initiatives that lower the barrier to adoption and shorten sales cycles. Modular pricing that ties cost to usage can provide the flexibility enterprises need when budgets are under pressure. Moreover, the emphasis will shift toward expanding existing accounts—cross‑selling, upselling, and deepening usage—to sustain revenue growth. Companies that have built robust expansion engines, such as those with high net‑retention rates above 120%, will be better positioned to weather the slowdown. Investors should watch for early signs of budget tightening in upcoming earnings calls and SEC filings. A rise in churn rates or a slowdown in expansion bookings could signal that the SaaS market is entering a more disciplined phase. Conversely, firms that can demonstrate clear ROI and flexible consumption models may capture market share from competitors caught flat‑footed. Home News [News] Intel Reportedly to Cut 103 Jobs in Mid-August After DCAI Layoff News Emerges 2026-07-30 Semiconductors editor Intel confirmed last week that it would launch a new round of layoffs in its Data Center and AI Group, though the company has yet to disclose the scale. New details have since surfaced, though Intel has not confirmed a direct link between the two. According to the Francisco Chronicle , Intel plans to cut 103 positions across four Bay Area offices next month, marking the latest workforce reduction at the Santa Clara-based chipmaker. The permanent layoffs, which will reportedly take effect Aug. 15, is expected to primarily impact Intel’s Santa Clara facilities, according to filings submitted to California authorities cited by the report. The Francisco Chronicle report adds that the largest reduction will come at the company’s SC-12 facility on Juliette Lane, where 67 employees will be affected, followed by 24 cuts at the Robert Noyce Building headquarters, 10 at another Juliette Lane office, and two at its Laurelwood Road location. The latest workforce reduction comes even as Intel’s data center business shows signs of recovery, driven by strong demand for server CPUs. According to Wccftech , citing Intel’s latest SEC filing , the company’s server CPU average selling prices (ASPs) surged 48% in the second quarter, fueled by a higher mix of premium products. Meanwhile, its Data Center and AI business recorded a 59% YoY revenue increase, generating US$6.3 billion in quarterly sales. According to The Oregonian/OregonLive , the company’s global workforce has contracted by nearly 40% since 2022, falling from approximately 132,000 employees to around 81,000 today. The decline reflects both portfolio changes, including business divestitures, and large-scale workforce reductions across global operations, the report says. Intel’s DCAI Reset Intel’s data center business has been in flux for over a year, well before this month’s layoff news. As Data Center Knowledge reported, CEO Lip-Bu Tan reshuffled his leadership bench back in September 2025, tapping former Arm executive Kevork Kechichian to run the newly reconstituted Data Center Group. According to Data Center Frontier , Intel’s Data Center and AI Group was split into two separate organizations, with the Data Center Group focusing on CPUs and the AI Group overseeing AI accelerators and related products. More significantly, the Data Center Group report directly to CEO Lip-Bu Tan, removing an additional layer of management introduced when Intel veteran Michelle Johnston Holthaus was appointed CEO of Intel Products, the report noted. Follow Peter DeSantis, Amazon's SVP of Foundational AI Models, Custom Silicon, and Quantum Computing Bloomberg/Getty Images 2026-07-28T09:00:01.288Z Read in app Copy link Email Facebook WhatsApp X LinkedIn Bluesky Threads Impact Link Save Saved Listen to this story Amazon is overhauling its AI strategy, winding down many in-house models, reorganizing teams, and focusing engineers on a new strategy to compete at the frontier, according to people familiar with the matter. The changes follow layoffs in Amazon's Artificial General Intelligence, or AGI , organization last week and the shutdown of AGI Lab, a research group it created in 2024 after hiring most of the team behind AI startup Adept. The restructuring suggests Amazon is refocusing its AI strategy. Rather than investing across a number of text, image, and video models, the company is concentrating engineering talent and scarce computing resources on its highest priorities. "KTLO" Amazon has begun deprecating most of its in-house flagship Nova models, including the high-end Premier and Omni models, Reel video-generation model, and Canvas image-generation model, according to people familiar with the matter. Some Amazon employees described these models as operating in "KTLO," short for "keep the lights on," an engineering term for software that remains supported for existing customers but is no longer a major development priority. FMR According to the people familiar with the matter, resources have increasingly moved away from the existing Nova models and toward a new frontier-model effort led by researcher Pieter Abbeel, who came to Amazon through the acquisition of AI robotics startup Covariant. Known internally as Frontier Model Research, or FMR, the initiative has become a top priority this year. Under that effort, Amazon is developing a new flagship foundation model that is expected to debut at this year's re:Invent annual conference, which typically happens in the fall. An Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider the company has long supported AI models in production for extended periods because customers depend on them, and said Amazon remains committed to investing in frontier models. "AI models remain one of the most important things we're working on, and that hasn't changed," the spokesperson said. "As with any AI portfolio, we continually evolve our model lineup based on what customers need, and we always provide customers clear guidance and migration paths as models advance." Explore BI Games Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. Play now Job cuts and departures The organizational change does not necessarily mean Amazon is abandoning Nova altogether. The remaining Nova portfolio includes the Nova 2 Sonic and Nova 2 Lite foundation models, Nova Forge, a service for building and customizing models, and Nova Act, Amazon's AI agent technology. Indeed, the new model that FMR is developing could emerge under the Nova brand. Instead, the shift reflects a broader reorganization of Amazon's AI efforts that has unfolded over the past year. Amazon created its AGI organization in 2023 to build foundation models and other technologies capable of powering future AI products across the company. Rohit Prasad , a longtime Alexa executive, led the organization until he departed in December 2025. The AGI organization oversaw several specialized groups. One was AGI Lab, which Amazon established in 2024 after hiring AI startup Adept's cofounders and licensing its technology. Led by Adept cofounder David Luan, the lab focused on long-term AI research. Luan left Amazon in February, and the company shut down the AGI Lab last week as part of the latest reorganization. Separately, Frontier Model Research was created within the AGI organization to develop Amazon's next generation of frontier AI models. After Prasad's departure, Amazon tapped Abbeel to lead the group. People familiar with the transition said FMR has since become the organization's primary focus. DeSantis narrows the focus The broader AGI organization was also reorganized. In December, Amazon placed it under senior vice president Peter DeSantis, combining it with the company's silicon development and quantum computing organizations. People familiar with the transition said DeSantis has pursued a more focused AI strategy than his predecessor. Under Prasad, Amazon pursued multiple model families spanning text, image, and video generation. DeSantis, however, has concentrated Amazon's engineering talent and computing resources on a smaller number of frontier-model efforts, they said. Employees said they have received little guidance about the long-term future of Nova models, fueling uncertainty across the organization. The layoffs surprised many employees, the people said, because frontier model researchers had long been among Amazon's most prized technical talent. Employees said AGI also operated differently from the rest of the company, maintaining separate leveling and compensation systems to compete more aggressively for AI talent. The changes mark a major shift in Amazon's AI ambitions. Just last year, AWS used its re:Invent conference to unveil Nova Omni 2 as its flagship multimodal reasoning model. In 2023, CEO Andy Jassy personally championed AGI as the team that would build Amazon's most ambitious foundation models , prompting the creation of six new research groups.
